overview: The East India Company grew from a trading corporation into a colonial territorial power in South Asia. This map’s 1815 to 1878 interval is misleading: Company government ended in 1858, and the corporation was dissolved in 1874.

periods.title: Trade before territorial empire
periods.summary: A royal charter in 1600 gave English merchants exclusive trading rights east of the Cape of Good Hope.

periods.title: Conquest and parliamentary intervention
periods.summary: Victories at Plassey and Buxar brought revenue power. A financial crisis in 1772 led to new parliamentary controls.

periods.title: Expansion under government supervision
periods.summary: The Board of Control monitored Company policy. Expansion later included annexations that angered Indian rulers and their followers.

periods.title: Rebellion
periods.summary: Soldiers, rulers and ordinary people challenged Company authority, while other Indians supported the British.

periods.title: After Company government
periods.summary: The Crown took over government in 1858. The corporation’s remaining legal existence ended in 1874.

sections.title: A corporation becomes a colonial power

items.text: The Company began as a trading enterprise, not as the government of India. Its seventeenth-century coastal posts included Surat, Bombay, Madras and Calcutta. Victories at Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764 helped turn commercial influence into control over revenues in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

British officials did not simply leave this enormous business alone. After the Company’s financial crisis, Parliament created a governor-general and council in 1773. The 1784 Board of Control added government supervision. Company rule combined private corporate interests with growing British state authority.

Company expansion could destroy rival courts. In 1799 its army stormed Seringapatam, killed Mysore’s ruler Tipu Sultan and looted the city. A wooden mechanical tiger from his palace was sent to London. Its hidden organ and moving arm show the inventiveness of Mysore’s craftspeople; its removal records the violence behind imperial museum collections.

Trade also linked suffering in different countries. Opium grown in India was sold onward by merchants into illegal trade with China. Chinese officials destroyed opium shipments in 1839; Britain went to war. Tea and other desirable goods were entangled with addictive drugs, coercion and the struggle over who could control trade.

sections.title: Ships, markets and things people made

items.text: Indian shipbuilders supplied the maritime skills behind overseas power. Jamsetjee Bomanjee Wadia worked at Bombay Dockyard and built ships for clients including the Company. A surviving portrait shows him holding the plan of HMS Minden, which he built for the Royal Navy in 1810. The man with the drawing helped make the fleet possible.

A sailor’s education could continue far from a classroom. Edward Barlow left home as a teenager, served in the Royal Navy and later joined the Company. While working in Asia he taught himself to write. His surviving journal preserves experiences aboard a Company ship during a life spanning the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries.

Indian artists earned money from European customers by painting local people, buildings, plants and occupations. These works are called Company paintings, although the patrons were not always Company employees. Artists combined Indian and European techniques, sometimes polishing imported paper with traditional burnishing methods. Even the paper could reveal an exchange of skills.

A picture titled A Doctor with a Female Patient, made in Lucknow around 1850, survives in an album of occupations. Conservators discovered that its white pigment had darkened and treated it to reveal the light blue background again. Lucknow then belonged to Awadh, before its annexation: Company painting describes a market and style, not a reliable political boundary.

In early nineteenth-century Calcutta, pilgrims visiting Kalighat created a market for inexpensive religious pictures. Painters adapted long storytelling scrolls into single sheets with a few figures and plain backgrounds. Cheaper paints and mill-made paper helped them work quickly. A souvenir could be affordable, portable and full of meaning; elaborate scenery was optional.

A silver rupee in Museums Victoria carries the original English words “EAST INDIA COMPANY” and “ONE RUPEE”. Below, Persian-script lettering is catalogued as Yek Rupiya, meaning “one rupee”. This is an attested bilingual coin sample: the English is reproduced in its original alphabet, while the Persian is given in the museum’s transliteration.

That coin displays 1835, but its small F mint mark identifies a Calcutta issue actually struck between 1836 and 1840. The older year was deliberately retained. A date on an object is evidence to investigate, not always its birthday! The same coin puts a British king on one face and the Company’s name on the other.

Waste disposal was a household responsibility as well as a public problem. A later official history of Madras records 1776 regulations requiring each house in George Town to have a cesspool and forbidding carts and cows from being kept in the streets. A cesspool collected waste; it was not a modern sewer connection. The rules show what authorities demanded, rather than proving every household complied.

Hindu College opened in Calcutta in 1817 for boys from Hindu families. Its subjects included Bengali, Sanskrit, English, history, astronomy, mathematics and chemistry. In 1855 it became the government-run Presidency College and admitted young men from different communities. This broadened one institution’s access, while girls still remained outside its classrooms.

Girls’ schooling had its own institutions and advocates. John Elliot Drinkwater Bethune established the Calcutta Female School in 1849. The later Bethune College traces its origins to that school, but the college itself dates to 1879. Keeping the dates separate matters: a girl attending the school during Company rule was not yet a university student.

Medical College, Bengal was founded in 1835. Its early students studied chemistry, pharmacy, botany, anatomy and clinical medicine. The 1837 to 1838 curriculum even included natural philosophy and the steam engine. Training doctors could involve plants, bodies and machines in the same course of study, while colonial policy increasingly sidelined older Indian systems of medicine.

Care expanded beyond lectures. The college’s new hospital building opened in 1852 with room for 350 patients. Such buildings gave students a place to learn from illness and gave patients an institution where they could receive treatment. The number describes that hospital’s planned accommodation, not the medical provision available to every family in Bengal.

Reports from the college describe ether and chloroform being used for operations soon after chloroform’s introduction to anesthesia in 1847. Students also practiced examining patients and recording what they found. These were examples of medical techniques being adopted and taught locally, not discoveries made by the Company itself.

Smallpox could frighten an entire household. In a report on Bengal vaccination during 1802 to 1803, John Shoolbred described parents’ anxiety and the scars and damaged eyesight the disease could leave in children. He was trying to persuade readers of vaccination’s value. His report preserves both a medical campaign and concern for families facing a dangerous illness.

Bengal’s famine of 1769 to 1770 also exposed conflicts over food and power. Company records preserved accusations and counteraccusations about grain monopolies and oppression during the crisis. A later proposal by Robert Kyd in 1786 suggested introducing food plants such as sago and date palms through a botanical garden to help prevent famine. Officials debated remedies, but a proposal is not proof that hunger was solved.

sections.title: Resistance and the end of Company rule

items.text: The rebellion of 1857 grew from several grievances. Indian soldiers resented pay, promotion and cultural disrespect, while rulers and their followers opposed annexations such as Awadh’s in 1856. Soldiers were joined by ordinary people. Other Indian rulers and military units supported the British, so this was also a period of difficult and divided loyalties.

The imported outline represents one coarse map snapshot, not an empire with unchanged borders until 1878. Its dates run through the 1858 transfer to Crown government and even past the corporation’s dissolution in 1874. Read later institutions under the British Raj card. The end of a company’s power did not end Indian communities, crafts or learning.

ending.text: Company government ended when the British Crown took over in 1858. The corporation was fully dissolved in 1874. Its political successor was Crown colonial rule, while the people and institutions of South Asia continued through that change.
